questions.title: Hypovolemic & Hemorrhagic Shock
questions.stem: What size NS/LR fluid bolus is given to an adult in hypovolemic or hemorrhagic shock?
questions.explanation: Adults get repeated 500 mL crystalloid boluses titrated to an SBP of 80 – 90 mmHg or a palpable radial pulse. The weight-based volumes are the pediatric and neonatal doses in the same band.

questions.title: Hypovolemic & Hemorrhagic Shock
questions.stem: In adult hemorrhagic shock, to what blood pressure endpoint are fluid boluses titrated?
questions.explanation: Permissive hypotension is the goal in hemorrhage: boluses are given to maintain an SBP of 80 – 90 mmHg or the presence of a radial pulse, not a normal pressure. An SBP of 80 mmHg is the pediatric target in the same guideline.

questions.title: Hypovolemic & Hemorrhagic Shock
questions.stem: How is the shock index calculated when assessing hypovolemic or hemorrhagic shock?
options: Heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure
Systolic blood pressure divided by heart rate
Heart rate divided by mean arterial pressure
Mean arterial pressure divided by heart rate
questions.explanation: Shock index is HR / SBP, and the higher the number the more severe the shock. The age-specific positive cut-offs are > 0.9 for age 13 and over, > 1.0 for ages 7 – 12, and > 1.22 for ages 4 – 6.

questions.title: Hypovolemic & Hemorrhagic Shock
questions.stem: In adult hypovolemic or hemorrhagic shock that persists after fluid resuscitation, what is the push-dose epinephrine dose?
questions.explanation: Push-dose epinephrine 5 – 20 mcg IV every 3 – 5 minutes is a temporizing measure only, used until an infusion is running. The 0.1 mL/kg push dose is the pediatric figure.

questions.title: Hypovolemic & Hemorrhagic Shock
questions.stem: An adult in hypovolemic or hemorrhagic shock remains hypotensive after adequate fluid resuscitation with a heart rate of 135. Which vasopressor infusion is preferred?
questions.explanation: Vasopressor choice in hypovolemic and hemorrhagic shock is split by rate: norepinephrine is preferred when the heart rate is 120 or above, epinephrine when it is below 120, because epinephrine's beta effect would worsen an already fast rate.

questions.title: Hypovolemic & Hemorrhagic Shock
questions.stem: In adult hypovolemic or hemorrhagic shock with no signs of pulmonary edema, what is the maximum volume of crystalloid?
questions.explanation: The ceiling for bleeding-related hypotension is 3 L absent pulmonary edema. The 2 – 4 L figure applies to hypotension unrelated to bleeding, such as gastroenteritis.

questions.title: Hypovolemic & Hemorrhagic Shock
questions.stem: What NS/LR bolus volume is given to a child in hypovolemic shock?
questions.explanation: Children get 20 mL/kg boluses to maintain an SBP of 80 mmHg or a brachial pulse. The 5 – 10 mL/kg bolus is reserved for when pulmonary edema is present, and 10 mL/kg is the neonatal bolus.

questions.title: Hypovolemic & Hemorrhagic Shock
questions.stem: A neonate in hypovolemic shock is receiving 10 mL/kg fluid boluses. What is the maximum total fluid volume?
questions.explanation: Neonates are bolused at 10 mL/kg up to a maximum of 30 mL/kg. The 20 – 60 mL/kg figure applies to pediatric hypotension unrelated to blood loss.

questions.title: Hypovolemic & Hemorrhagic Shock
questions.stem: Which resuscitation fluid should be avoided in neonates with hypovolemic shock?
questions.explanation: The Hypovolemic & Hemorrhagic Shock guideline specifically says to avoid lactated Ringers in neonates when giving 10 mL/kg boluses; normal saline is the fluid of choice in that population.

questions.title: Hypovolemic & Hemorrhagic Shock
questions.stem: In pediatric hypovolemic or hemorrhagic shock, in what unit must IV push doses of epinephrine be dosed and documented?
questions.explanation: The guideline explicitly requires pediatric push-dose epinephrine to be both dosed and documented in mL/kg (0.1 mL/kg of the 10 mcg/mL concentration), which removes a common decimal-point error at the bedside.

questions.title: Hypovolemic & Hemorrhagic Shock
questions.stem: In hypovolemic or hemorrhagic shock, to what maximum rate may a norepinephrine infusion be titrated?
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine is titrated every 3 – 5 minutes to a maximum of 45 mcg/min; the 2 mcg/kg/min ceiling belongs to epinephrine in the same band.

questions.title: Ischemic Stroke - TSE
questions.stem: A patient with a suspected ischemic stroke has no signs of respiratory distress. At what SpO2 should supplemental oxygen be applied?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is withheld in stroke unless there is respiratory distress or the SpO2 falls below 94%; routine oxygen offers no benefit and hyperoxia may worsen ischemic injury.

questions.title: Ischemic Stroke - TSE
questions.stem: The initial stroke screen on a patient with suspected stroke is negative. What should the crew do?
options: Stop here and transport per local destination protocol
Transport to the closest comprehensive stroke center
Repeat the stroke screen in 15 minutes
questions.explanation: A negative initial screen means a stroke is unlikely: the guideline says STOP HERE, transport per local destination protocol, and do not continue in the ischemic stroke PCG. The LVO severity screen is performed only after a positive initial screen.

questions.title: Ischemic Stroke - TSE
questions.stem: Which stroke severity (LVO) screening tool is specified for Washington?
questions.explanation: The LVO tool varies by state: LAMS in Washington, BEFAST in Oregon, C-STAT in Hawaii, and VAN in Montana and (by recommendation) Idaho.

questions.title: Ischemic Stroke - TSE
questions.stem: How should a patient with an ischemic stroke be positioned for transport?
questions.explanation: Flat supine positioning maximises cerebral perfusion to the ischemic penumbra. Only if the patient cannot tolerate lying flat is minimal head elevation provided.

questions.title: Ischemic Stroke - TSE
questions.stem: How often must serial neurological examinations be documented in an ischemic stroke patient?
questions.explanation: Serial neuro exams every 15 minutes are what detect deterioration from ICH or herniation in transit; the same 15-minute interval is used to check for oral angioedema during and after alteplase.

questions.title: Ischemic Stroke - TSE
questions.stem: At what temperature should ALS crews remove sources of heat and consider antipyretics in an ischemic stroke patient?
questions.explanation: Even mild hyperthermia worsens ischemic brain injury, so the trigger for cooling and acetaminophen in stroke is a low 99.5°F (37.5°C) — well below the fever thresholds used in hyperthermia or sepsis.

questions.title: Ischemic Stroke - TSE
questions.stem: A 70 kg adult with an ischemic stroke has a temperature of 100.8°F. What acetaminophen dose is given?
questions.explanation: Adults over 50 kg get 1000 mg IV over 15 minutes, repeatable every 6 hours. Patients at or under 50 kg are dosed at 15 mg/kg to a maximum single dose of 750 mg.

questions.title: Ischemic Stroke - TSE
questions.stem: What vascular access should ALS crews establish in an ischemic stroke patient?
options: 18 gauge or larger in a proximal site
Intraosseous access in the proximal tibia
A saline lock in the hand or wrist
questions.explanation: An 18 gauge or larger catheter in a proximal site is specified because the receiving facility will need it for CT angiography contrast and thrombolytic administration.

questions.title: Ischemic Stroke - TSE
questions.stem: An ischemic stroke patient who has already received thrombolytics has a blood pressure of 192/98. What does the CCT stroke blood pressure algorithm direct?
options: Reduce the BP to a target of 180/105
Reduce the BP by no more than 15%
Treat only if the SBP exceeds 220
questions.explanation: Once thrombolytics are on board, the algorithm treats any SBP above 180 or DBP above 105 down to a target of 180/105 to limit hemorrhagic conversion. The 15% reduction rule applies to patients who are not thrombolytic candidates.

questions.title: Ischemic Stroke - TSE
questions.stem: An ischemic stroke patient who is not a thrombolytic candidate and has not received thrombolytics has a blood pressure of 236/118. What does the CCT stroke blood pressure algorithm direct?
options: Reduce the BP by no more than 15%
Reduce the BP to a target of 180/105
Reduce the BP to a target of 140/90
questions.explanation: For a non-candidate the algorithm treats only when the SBP exceeds 220 or the DBP exceeds 120, and then lowers the pressure by no more than 15%, because dropping it to target values may be harmful in an unreperfused brain.

questions.title: Ischemic Stroke - TSE
questions.stem: When treating hypotension in an ischemic stroke patient, what perfusion targets should CCT crews maintain?
options: SBP above 100/70 with a MAP above 80
SBP of 90 plus twice the age in years
questions.explanation: Hypotension is as dangerous as hypertension in ischemic stroke; fluids and vasopressors are used to hold the SBP above 100/70 and the MAP above 80 to preserve collateral flow to the penumbra.

questions.title: Ischemic Stroke - TSE
questions.stem: In ischemic stroke, what is the general time window from last known well for IV thrombolytics?
questions.explanation: IV thrombolytics are given up to 4.5 hours from LKW, with facility arrival and entry through the doors by 4 hours so there is time to evaluate and treat.

questions.title: Ischemic Stroke - TSE
questions.stem: For endovascular thrombectomy in ischemic stroke, by how many hours from last known well must the patient arrive at the facility?
questions.explanation: The thrombectomy window is 24 hours from LKW, but the patient must be at the facility by 22 hours so there is time for evaluation and the procedure inside the 24-hour limit.

questions.title: Ischemic Stroke - TSE
questions.stem: A suspected stroke patient has a negative VAN or C-STAT screen. How much extra transport time is acceptable to reach a higher-level stroke center?
questions.explanation: A negative LVO screen means thrombectomy is unlikely to help, so bypass is allowed only if it adds no more than 30 minutes — and never if the added time pushes the patient outside the 4.5-hour thrombolytic window.

questions.title: Ischemic Stroke - TSE
questions.stem: In the Washington prehospital stroke triage procedure, what stroke severity score triggers transport to an endovascular-capable center?
questions.explanation: The Washington procedure uses LAMS (maximum 5 points). A score of 4 or more, combined with time since last known well, directs transport to a Level I or Level II center with endovascular capability.

questions.title: Ischemic Stroke - TSE
questions.stem: A stroke patient on an alteplase drip develops orolingual angioedema. After stopping the infusion, what methylprednisolone dose is given?
questions.explanation: The angioedema sequence is stop the alteplase, then methylprednisolone 125 mg IV and diphenhydramine 50 mg IV. Hydrocortisone 100 mg is the septic shock steroid dose, not this one.

questions.title: Ischemic Stroke - TSE
questions.stem: In a stroke patient, orolingual angioedema continues to worsen after alteplase is stopped and steroids and diphenhydramine are given. What is the next treatment?
options: A second dose of diphenhydramine 50 mg IV
questions.explanation: Worsening angioedema gets epinephrine 0.3 mg (0.3 mL of 1 mg/mL) IM, with the caveat that there is a theoretical ICH risk from the resulting rise in blood pressure. Severe angioedema may require intubation.

questions.title: Ischemic Stroke - TSE
questions.stem: Which agents must never be used to lower blood pressure in a known or suspected stroke patient?
questions.explanation: Nitroglycerin and nifedipine cause abrupt, unpredictable drops in pressure and cerebral vasodilation. Labetalol and nicardipine are the two agents the CCT algorithm actually lists.

questions.title: Ischemic Stroke - TSE
questions.stem: Which stroke center designation can perform mechanical thrombectomy but is not a Comprehensive Stroke Center?
options: Acute Stroke Ready Hospital, level III
questions.explanation: A TSC (level II+) performs clot removal and post-procedure care. A PSC gives IV thrombolytics but not thrombectomy, and an ASRH diagnoses, stabilizes, gives tPA and transfers onward.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: How should BLS crews deliver oxygen to a patient with carbon monoxide poisoning?
options: Titrate oxygen to an SpO2 of 94%
Nasal cannula titrated to work of breathing
questions.explanation: Carboxyhemoglobin is read as saturated by a standard pulse oximeter, so the guideline for carbon monoxide poisoning directs maximum-flow 100% oxygen and explicitly says not to base the oxygen need on SpO2 values.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: What is the adult intranasal naloxone dose for opioid overdose?
questions.explanation: Adults get naloxone 0.4 mg IN, repeated every 3 – 5 minutes. The 0.1 mg/kg figure is the pediatric dose, and 5 mg is the per-dose maximum used in clonidine overdose.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: What is the pediatric intranasal naloxone dose for suspected opioid overdose with respiratory depression?
questions.explanation: Children get 0.1 mg/kg IN, repeated every 3 – 5 minutes, with a maximum single dose of 0.4 mg and a maximum total of 5 mg. The flat 0.4 mg is the adult dose.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: For BLS crews, what is the maximum total naloxone dose for a pediatric opioid overdose?
questions.explanation: Pediatric intranasal naloxone has two ceilings: a maximum single dose of 0.4 mg and a maximum total of 5 mg. The 10 mg total belongs to the clonidine overdose regimen at the CCT level.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: To what endpoint is naloxone titrated in opioid overdose?
options: Return of a normal pupil size
questions.explanation: The guideline states the endpoint twice: titrate to respiratory effort, NOT mental status. Waking the patient fully risks acute withdrawal, agitation and a combative patient in a confined aircraft.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: Under what circumstance may naloxone be administered in flight for an opioid overdose?
options: Only if the patient has cardiovascular collapse from narcotics
Any time the respiratory rate falls below 10
Only after the airway has been secured
Only with online medical control approval
questions.explanation: Crews are directed not to give naloxone in flight unless the patient has cardiovascular collapse from narcotics, which is rare; an abrupt reversal in a confined cabin is more dangerous than continued support of ventilation.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: On an interfacility transfer of a poisoned patient, within what time frame of the toxic exposure should ALS crews consider activated charcoal?
questions.explanation: Charcoal is considered, after consultation with the sending provider, if the exposure was within the last 2 hours. The 4-hour window is specific to acetaminophen ingestion.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: What mental status requirement must a poisoned patient meet before activated charcoal is given?
options: Awake and alert, or intubated first and given via NG
Any mental status, provided it is given via NG tube
Alert enough to follow commands for 30 minutes
Awake, with online medical control approval only
questions.explanation: Charcoal aspiration is devastating, so the patient must be awake and alert; a patient with an altered level of consciousness must be intubated before charcoal is given via nasogastric tube.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: What activated charcoal dose and maximum are given for an anticholinergic overdose?
questions.explanation: The anticholinergic indication is 1 gram/kg to a maximum of 50 grams, given only with sending provider or medical control consult and only with an intact mental status or a secured airway. The general overdose entry allows 50 – 100 grams.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: How is an adult sodium bicarbonate infusion mixed and run for anticholinergic or tricyclic overdose?
options: 150 mEq in 850 mL D5W, infused at 200 mL/hr
3 amps in 850 mL D5W, infused at 250 mL/hr
150 mEq in 1 L NS, infused at 250 mL/hr
3 amps in 1 L D5W, infused at 200 mL/hr
questions.explanation: The standard alkalinization mix is 150 mEq of bicarbonate in 850 mL of D5W, given as a 50 mEq bolus and then run at 200 mL/hr. The 3-amp/850 mL at 250 mL/hr mix is the salicylate and phenobarbital regimen.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: What glucagon dose is given for a beta blocker overdose?
questions.explanation: Glucagon 5 – 10 mg slow IV push bypasses the beta receptor to raise intracellular cAMP. The 2 – 5 mg figure is atropine for organophosphates and 3 grams is calcium gluconate.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: What insulin regimen is used for refractory hypotension in beta blocker overdose?
questions.explanation: High-dose insulin euglycemia therapy starts with regular insulin 1 unit/kg plus dextrose 10% 250 mL, then an infusion at 0.5 units/kg/hr titrated every 15 – 30 minutes up to 2 units/kg/hr based on cardiac and blood pressure response.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: In beta blocker overdose, which electrolyte abnormality must be corrected before starting high-dose insulin therapy?
questions.explanation: Insulin drives potassium intracellularly, so hypokalemia is corrected first unless the patient is in extremis or arrest. Potassium is then measured hourly and treated if below 3.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: What adult calcium gluconate dose is given for calcium channel blocker overdose?
questions.explanation: Calcium gluconate 3 grams slow IV push over 2 minutes, repeatable every 15 minutes twice, is the CCB dose. The 1 – 3 gram figure is for magnesium sulfate toxicity and 10 – 30 mg/kg is its pediatric equivalent.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: What naloxone dose is given for clonidine overdose with respiratory depression and altered mental status?
questions.explanation: Clonidine overdose needs much larger naloxone doses than opioid overdose: 0.1 mg/kg IV repeated every 1 – 2 minutes, to a maximum of 5 mg per dose and 10 mg total.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: What adult hydroxocobalamin dose is given for cyanide poisoning?
questions.explanation: Adults get hydroxocobalamin 5 grams IV over 15 minutes alongside 100% oxygen; 70 mg/kg is the pediatric dose for the same indication.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: What pediatric hydroxocobalamin dose is given for cyanide poisoning?
questions.explanation: Children get 70 mg/kg IV over 15 minutes. The 20 – 50 mg/kg figure is pediatric pralidoxime and 10 – 30 mg/kg is pediatric calcium gluconate for magnesium toxicity.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: What adult atropine dose is given for organophosphate poisoning?
questions.explanation: Organophosphate poisoning needs far more atropine than bradycardia does: 2 – 5 mg slow IV push or IM, repeated every 5 minutes until secretions decrease. The 1 mg dose and 0.04 mg/kg ceiling belong to beta blocker and calcium channel blocker bradycardia.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: In organophosphate poisoning, to what endpoint is atropine repeated?
options: Until the maximum of 0.04 mg/kg is reached
questions.explanation: Atropine is repeated every 5 minutes until secretions decrease — drying the airway is the therapeutic endpoint, not heart rate or pupil size, and there is no fixed ceiling in this indication.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: What adult pralidoxime (2-PAM) dose is given for organophosphate poisoning?
questions.explanation: Pralidoxime 1 – 2 grams in 100 mL NS over 15 – 30 minutes reactivates acetylcholinesterase, complementing atropine's receptor blockade. The weight-based 20 – 50 mg/kg is the pediatric dose.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: Which paralytic should be used for RSI in organophosphate poisoning?
questions.explanation: Organophosphates inhibit plasma cholinesterase, so succinylcholine's action is markedly prolonged. Rocuronium is directed instead when RSI is required.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: What sodium bicarbonate bolus is given for salicylate poisoning?
questions.explanation: Salicylate poisoning gets a 2 mEq/kg bicarbonate bolus followed by an infusion of 3 amps in 850 mL D5W at 250 mL/hr, with attention to volume resuscitation and urine output. The 1 mEq/kg bolus is the pediatric tricyclic dose.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: What flumazenil dose is given for an iatrogenic benzodiazepine overdose?
questions.explanation: Flumazenil 0.2 mg IV over 15 seconds, repeatable with another 0.2 mg if there is no response after 45 seconds, to a maximum of 1 mg.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: For which benzodiazepine overdoses is the use of flumazenil restricted?
options: Overdoses with a QRS above 100 msec
questions.explanation: Flumazenil is restricted to iatrogenic benzodiazepine overdoses, because reversal in a chronic user or a mixed ingestion can precipitate refractory seizures.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: In sympathomimetic overdose, above what blood pressure is benzodiazepine-refractory hypertension treated?
questions.explanation: Hypertension from cocaine, amphetamines or MDMA usually responds to benzodiazepines; nitroglycerin or nitroprusside are added only for pressures above 210/120 that remain refractory.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: At what rate is a nitroglycerin infusion started for refractory hypertension in sympathomimetic overdose?
questions.explanation: Nitroglycerin starts at 10 mcg/min and is titrated every 5 minutes to effect or a maximum of 400 mcg/min. The 0.3 mcg/kg/min figure is the nitroprusside starting rate.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: Above what QRS duration is alkalinization indicated in tricyclic antidepressant overdose?
questions.explanation: A QRS above 100 msec, together with hypotension, seizures or life-threatening arrhythmias, calls for alkalinization or hyperventilation to a pH of 7.45 – 7.55 to overcome sodium channel blockade. A QRS above 160 msec doubles the bicarbonate bolus.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: An adult with a tricyclic overdose has a QRS of 180 msec and no D5W is available for an infusion. What sodium bicarbonate bolus is given?
questions.explanation: The bolus-only schedule gives 50 mEq for a QRS of 100 – 160 msec, HR above 140, hypotension or seizures, and doubles it to 100 mEq once the QRS exceeds 160 msec.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: A 15 kg child with a tricyclic overdose needs a weight-based sodium bicarbonate infusion. At what rate is it run?
options: 8 mL/kg/hr for the first 10 kg, then 4 mL/kg/hr
4 mL/kg/hr for the first 10 kg, then 8 mL/kg/hr
120 mL/kg, plus 2 mL/kg/hr for weight over 20 kg
2 mL/kg/hr for the first 20 kg of body weight
questions.explanation: Under 20 kg the infusion runs at 8 mL/kg/hr for the first 10 kg and 4 mL/kg/hr for the remaining 10 – 20 kg. At 20 kg and above it becomes 120 mL/kg plus 2 mL/kg/hr for the weight over 20 kg, capped at 200 mL/hr.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: When starting a vasopressor for severe hypotension in a pediatric tricyclic overdose, what minimum systolic blood pressure is the target?
options: 90 plus twice the age in years
80 plus twice the age in years
70 plus twice the age in years
questions.explanation: For hypotension unresponsive to fluids and bicarbonate, norepinephrine or epinephrine is started at 0.05 mcg/kg/min and titrated to maintain a minimum SBP of 90 + (2 x age in years).

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: In acetaminophen overdose, what level drawn 4 hours post-ingestion reflects possible toxicity?
questions.explanation: A 4-hour level above 150 mcg/mL (greater than 993 micromol/L) reflects possible toxicity. An overdose of as few as 20 standard-dose tablets can produce fatal hepatotoxicity.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: Which symptom pattern is typical of clonidine overdose?
options: CNS depression, bradycardia, hypotension and small pupils
Tachycardia, hypertension, dilated pupils and agitation
Salivation, bronchorrhea, miosis and muscle fasciculation
questions.explanation: Clonidine overdose mimics opioid intoxication — lethargy or coma, bradycardia, hypotension, respiratory depression and small pupils — which is why naloxone is the listed treatment, albeit at 0.1 mg/kg.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: For which ingestion is activated charcoal not indicated?
questions.explanation: Charcoal does not bind alcohols, petroleum products, corrosives or ionic compounds such as lithium and iron, and aspiration of a hydrocarbon is far worse than the ingestion. It is specifically directed for acetaminophen, salicylate and anticholinergic ingestions.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: Above what serum salicylate level may toxicity be present?
questions.explanation: Salicylate values above 40 mg/dL (2.9 mmol/L) may be associated with toxicity, but levels can be falsely reassuring in chronic ingestions. Fatal intoxication can follow 10 – 30 g in an adult or as little as 3 g in a child.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: What acid-base picture do adults with acute salicylate poisoning usually present with?
options: Mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis
Mixed respiratory acidosis and metabolic alkalosis
questions.explanation: Salicylates both stimulate the respiratory centre and uncouple oxidative phosphorylation, producing a mixed respiratory alkalosis with metabolic acidosis — which is why intubating these patients is dangerous and is reserved for clear respiratory failure.

questions.title: Poisoning & Overdoses
questions.stem: In a pregnant patient with carbon monoxide poisoning, above what carboxyhemoglobin level is hyperbaric oxygen indicated?
questions.explanation: Pregnancy lowers the threshold: COHb above 20% is an indication in a pregnant patient, versus above 25% otherwise. Loss of consciousness, new neurologic deficits and end-organ ischemia are also indications.

questions.title: Seizures
questions.stem: Chin-lift, jaw thrust and suction have not relieved airway obstruction in a seizing patient. What should BLS crews do next?
options: Place an OPA or NPA and ventilate via BVM as needed
Insert a bite block between the teeth
Place the patient in the recovery position
Proceed directly to rapid sequence induction
questions.explanation: An airway adjunct and BVM ventilation are the BLS answer; the guideline also says not to force anything between the teeth, which is the classic harmful reflex in a seizing patient.

questions.title: Seizures
questions.stem: What is the adult lorazepam dose for an actively seizing patient?
questions.explanation: Adults get lorazepam 2 – 4 mg IV or IM, repeatable every 5 minutes. The 0.1 mg/kg figure is the pediatric lorazepam dose and 0.3 mg/kg is intranasal midazolam.

questions.title: Seizures
questions.stem: What is the midazolam dose when given IV, IO or IM for an active seizure?
questions.explanation: Midazolam is 0.1 mg/kg by IV, IO or IM route and 0.3 mg/kg intranasally, repeatable every 5 minutes to a maximum single dose of 10 mg. IM is preferred when there is no IV access.

questions.title: Seizures
questions.stem: What is the intranasal midazolam dose for an active seizure?
questions.explanation: The intranasal dose is three times the IV dose at 0.3 mg/kg, and the guideline directs the volume be split between both nostrils to improve absorption.

questions.title: Seizures
questions.stem: When treating an active seizure, what is the maximum single dose of midazolam?
questions.explanation: Midazolam has a 10 mg maximum single dose regardless of route. The 4 mg figure is the top of the adult lorazepam range and 5 minutes is the repeat interval.

questions.title: Seizures
questions.stem: How should an intranasal midazolam dose be delivered to a seizing patient?
options: Into one nostril, then flushed with saline
questions.explanation: Splitting the dose between both nostrils halves the volume per side, which keeps it within what the nasal mucosa can absorb rather than running down the posterior pharynx.

questions.title: Seizures
questions.stem: If rocuronium or another long-acting paralytic is used in a seizing patient, what is required?
options: The patient remains adequately sedated beyond the paralytic's duration of action
The paralytic is reversed as soon as the airway is secured
A benzodiazepine infusion is started before the paralytic
Continuous EEG monitoring is established before transport
questions.explanation: A paralytic stops the convulsion but not the seizure, so sedation must outlast the paralysis. The Seizures guideline prefers avoiding long-acting blockers entirely because they mask ongoing seizure activity.

questions.title: Seizures
questions.stem: What is the pediatric lorazepam dose for an actively seizing child?
questions.explanation: Children get lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV or IM, repeatable every 5 minutes — the same weight-based figure as IV/IM midazolam. The 2 – 4 mg flat dose is the adult regimen.

questions.title: Seizures
questions.stem: A child who has been seizing is febrile. What acetaminophen dose is given?
questions.explanation: Fever lowers the seizure threshold in children, so acetaminophen 15 mg/kg IV over 15 minutes is given to a maximum of 750 mg. The 50 mg/kg figure is levetiracetam.

questions.title: Seizures
questions.stem: What ketamine dose is given for seizures refractory to benzodiazepines?
questions.explanation: Ketamine 1 mg/kg IV may be repeated every 5 minutes to a maximum of 5 mg/kg. The 15 – 20 mg/kg range belongs to fosphenytoin and phenobarbital, and 50 mg/kg to levetiracetam.

questions.title: Seizures
questions.stem: What is the maximum total ketamine dose for refractory seizures?
questions.explanation: Ketamine is repeated every 5 minutes from a starting 1 mg/kg to a cumulative ceiling of 5 mg/kg.

questions.title: Seizures
questions.stem: For seizures, what are the adult and pediatric maximum levetiracetam doses?
questions.explanation: Levetiracetam is 50 mg/kg infused over 15 minutes, capped at 3000 mg in adults and 1500 mg in children. The 2000 mg ceiling belongs to fosphenytoin and 1000 mg to phenobarbital.

questions.title: Seizures
questions.stem: What is the maximum fosphenytoin dose for refractory seizures?
questions.explanation: Fosphenytoin is 15 – 20 mg/kg infused at 150 mg/min to a maximum of 2000 mg. Phenobarbital shares the 15 – 20 mg/kg dose but runs at 60 mg/min with a 1000 mg ceiling.

questions.title: Seizures
questions.stem: What phenobarbital dose and maximum are given for refractory seizures?
questions.explanation: Phenobarbital 15 – 20 mg/kg is infused at 60 mg/min to a maximum of 1000 mg. The identical weight range with a 2000 mg ceiling is fosphenytoin, infused faster at 150 mg/min.

questions.title: Seizures
questions.stem: A patient in the third trimester of pregnancy is seizing. Which guideline should the crew follow?
options: General OB Care and Transport Considerations
questions.explanation: Third-trimester and post-partum seizures are treated as eclampsia until proven otherwise, which changes the drug from a benzodiazepine to magnesium sulfate.

questions.title: Seizures
questions.stem: What is the management for a seizing neonate?
options: Supportive care and treatment of the underlying cause
Benzodiazepines at the same weight-based dose as older children
Immediate loading with levetiracetam at 50 mg/kg
Intubation and a phenobarbital load before transport
questions.explanation: Neonatal seizures are usually driven by a reversible cause such as hypoglycemia, so the emphasis is supportive care and treating the etiology; benzodiazepines are reserved for prolonged seizures.

questions.title: Sepsis & Septic Shock - TSE
questions.stem: What NS/LR bolus volume is given at the ALS level to an adult with septic shock?
questions.explanation: ALS gives 500 mL boluses to a maximum of 3 L absent pulmonary edema. The 30 mL/kg figure is the CCT trigger-based bolus used for a MAP at or under 65 or a lactate of 4 or more.

questions.title: Sepsis & Septic Shock - TSE
questions.stem: In adult sepsis and septic shock, to what mean arterial pressure is fluid resuscitation titrated?
questions.explanation: A MAP above 65 mmHg is the resuscitation endpoint in sepsis — distinct from the permissive SBP of 80 – 90 used in hemorrhage and the MAP above 80 used in ischemic stroke.

questions.title: Sepsis & Septic Shock - TSE
questions.stem: At what rate is norepinephrine started in an adult with fluid-unresponsive septic shock?
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine starts at 2 – 10 mcg/min or 0.05 mcg/kg/min and is titrated every 3 – 5 minutes to a maximum of 45 mcg/min or 2 mcg/kg/min, with a second vasopressor added once the rate reaches 40 mcg/min.

questions.title: Sepsis & Septic Shock - TSE
questions.stem: What acetaminophen dose is given for an untreated fever in an adult with sepsis?
options: 1000 mg IV over 15 minutes q 6 hours
15 mg/kg IV to a max of 750 mg
750 mg IV over 15 minutes q 6 hours
500 mg IV over 15 minutes q 6 hours
questions.explanation: Adults get 1000 mg IV over 15 minutes every 6 hours; patients at or under 50 kg are dosed at 15 mg/kg to a maximum of 750 mg.

questions.title: Sepsis & Septic Shock - TSE
questions.stem: What NS/LR bolus volume is given to a child with septic shock?
questions.explanation: Children get 20 mL/kg boluses titrated to an SBP of 90 + (age x 2); neonates are limited to 10 mL/kg boluses to a maximum of 30 mL/kg.

questions.title: Sepsis & Septic Shock - TSE
questions.stem: Which vasopressor is first line for a child with fluid-unresponsive septic shock?
questions.explanation: Pediatric septic shock is more often myocardial in origin, so epinephrine at 0.05 mcg/kg/min is first line in children, whereas norepinephrine leads in adults.

questions.title: Sepsis & Septic Shock - TSE
questions.stem: In pediatric septic shock, to what systolic blood pressure are fluid boluses titrated?
options: 90 plus twice the age in years
80 plus twice the age in years
questions.explanation: The age-adjusted target of 90 + (age x 2) accounts for the normal rise in systolic pressure with age; the flat 80 – 90 mmHg target belongs to adult hemorrhagic shock.

questions.title: Sepsis & Septic Shock - TSE
questions.stem: Why is a pressure bag or a push-pull syringe method suggested for pediatric fluid boluses in septic shock?
options: Because IV pump flow rate limits slow rapid bolus delivery
Because it reduces the risk of fluid overload
Because it avoids the need for a second IV site
Because it allows accurate measurement of small volumes
questions.explanation: Pumps cap flow rates well below what a critically ill child needs, so the guideline directs a pressure bag or manual push-pull via syringe to actually deliver a rapid bolus.

questions.title: Sepsis & Septic Shock - TSE
questions.stem: An adult with sepsis has a MAP of 62 and a lactate of 5 mmol/L. What fluid bolus is given at the CCT level?
questions.explanation: A MAP at or below 65 or a lactate at or above 4 mmol/L triggers 30 mL/kg boluses, and more than 3 – 4 L may be required; HR, SpO2, RR and urine output are reassessed for adequate perfusion.

questions.title: Sepsis & Septic Shock - TSE
questions.stem: In septic shock, what vasopressin dose is given when adding it to fluids and other vasopressors?
questions.explanation: Vasopressin is given as a fixed, non-titrated 0.03 units/min; the other rates belong to epinephrine or norepinephrine and to nitroprusside.

questions.title: Sepsis & Septic Shock - TSE
questions.stem: At what rate is a dopamine infusion started in septic shock, and in which patients?
options: 5 mcg/kg/min, in highly selective bradycardic patients
20 mcg/kg/min, in patients already on norepinephrine
questions.explanation: Dopamine starts at 5 mcg/kg/min and is titrated to a maximum of 20 mcg/kg/min, but in septic shock it is restricted to highly selective patients with bradycardia because of its arrhythmogenic profile.

questions.title: Sepsis & Septic Shock - TSE
questions.stem: In septic shock, hypotension has persisted for over an hour despite adequate fluid and vasopressors. Which steroid and dose are given first?
questions.explanation: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV is the first choice for suspected critical illness-related corticosteroid insufficiency; methylprednisolone 125 mg IV is used only if hydrocortisone is unavailable.

questions.title: Sepsis & Septic Shock - TSE
questions.stem: How many SIRS criteria, with a suspected infection, are required for a clinical diagnosis of sepsis in an adult?
questions.explanation: Suspected infection plus two or more SIRS criteria makes the clinical diagnosis. The criteria are temperature above 38c or below 36c, HR above 90, RR above 20 or PaCO2 below 32, and WBC above 12,000, below 4,000, or more than 10% bands.

questions.title: Sepsis & Septic Shock - TSE
questions.stem: In screening for sepsis, what heart rate meets a SIRS criterion?
questions.explanation: A heart rate above 90 bpm is one of the four SIRS criteria, along with the temperature, respiratory rate or PaCO2, and white cell count criteria.

questions.title: Sepsis & Septic Shock - TSE
questions.stem: What role does hypotension play in diagnosing pediatric septic shock?
options: It is not necessary for the diagnosis, but its presence is confirmatory
It is required before septic shock can be diagnosed
It is only relevant in children under one year of age
It must be present on two consecutive readings
questions.explanation: Children compensate until they crash, so septic shock is diagnosed on signs of inadequate perfusion — altered mental status, urine output under 1 mL/kg/hr, mottled or cool extremities — with hypotension only confirming it.

questions.title: Childbirth - Uncomplicated
questions.stem: A term infant is delivered, breathing and vigorous and needs no resuscitation. When should the umbilical cord be clamped and cut?
questions.explanation: Delayed clamping at 1 to 3 minutes allows placental transfusion in an infant who does not need resuscitation. If resuscitation is needed, the cord may be clamped and cut as soon as necessary.

questions.title: Childbirth - Uncomplicated
questions.stem: During an uncomplicated childbirth, how far from the infant should the umbilical cord be clamped and cut?
options: At the level of the umbilicus
questions.explanation: The cord is clamped and cut about 6 inches from the infant, leaving enough length for umbilical venous access at the receiving facility. The 2-inch figure is the spacing between the two clamps.

questions.title: Childbirth - Uncomplicated
questions.stem: After an uncomplicated delivery, when should a newborn's nose and mouth be suctioned?
options: Only if unable to maintain a patent airway
Routinely, mouth first and then nose
Only if the amniotic fluid is meconium stained
Only if the five-minute APGAR is below 7
questions.explanation: Routine suctioning causes vagally mediated bradycardia and offers no benefit, so it is reserved for an infant who cannot maintain a patent airway — including infants born through meconium.

questions.title: Childbirth - Uncomplicated
questions.stem: At what points should a newborn be assessed using APGAR?
options: At the time of birth and five minutes later
At one minute and five minutes
At five minutes and ten minutes
At one, five and ten minutes
questions.explanation: The Childbirth - Uncomplicated guideline specifies assessment at the time of birth and again five minutes later, and adds that resuscitation must never be delayed in order to obtain an APGAR.

questions.title: Childbirth - Uncomplicated
questions.stem: How should a newborn's APGAR assessment be documented?
options: Describe the infant using the criteria rather than a numerical score
Record only the total score at birth and at five minutes
Record the score and the time resuscitation was started
Record the score only if it is below 7
questions.explanation: Documenting the actual findings — colour, tone, respiratory effort — carries more information to the receiving team than a single number, and avoids a score being disputed later.

questions.title: Childbirth - Uncomplicated
questions.stem: During childbirth, a nuchal cord cannot be unwrapped from the newborn's neck. What should be done?
options: Attach two umbilical clamps and cut the cord between them
Push the infant back up the birth canal
Deliver the infant through the loop of cord
Clamp the cord once and await the placenta
questions.explanation: If the cord cannot be slipped over the head it must be double-clamped and divided so the delivery can proceed; leaving it tight risks avulsion and fetal hypoxia.

questions.title: Childbirth - Uncomplicated
questions.stem: After an uncomplicated vaginal delivery, what volume of blood loss is considered significant postpartum hemorrhage?
questions.explanation: Blood loss above 500 mL calls for continued uterine massage, treatment for shock and an update to the receiving facility.

questions.title: Childbirth - Uncomplicated
questions.stem: During an uncomplicated delivery, how are the shoulders delivered once the head has emerged?
options: Guide the head downward for the anterior shoulder, then lift upward for the posterior shoulder
Lift the head upward for the anterior shoulder, then guide downward for the posterior shoulder
Apply steady traction straight outward until both shoulders deliver
Rotate the head 90 degrees and deliver both shoulders together
questions.explanation: The head is gently guided posteriorly until the anterior shoulder clears the pubic symphysis, then lifted anteriorly to deliver the posterior shoulder over the perineum.

questions.title: Childbirth - Uncomplicated
questions.stem: In the APGAR scoring table for a newborn, which pulse range earns 2 points?
questions.explanation: A pulse of 100 – 140 scores 2 points, below 100 scores 1 and an absent pulse scores 0, in the same way appearance, grimace, tone and respiration each score 0 to 2.

questions.title: Delivery Complications
questions.stem: In what position should a patient with a prolapsed cord be placed?
questions.explanation: Knee-chest takes the presenting part off the cord; lateral decubitus is accepted only if needed to secure the patient for ambulance transport. McRoberts is the shoulder dystocia manoeuvre.

questions.title: Delivery Complications
questions.stem: In a prolapsed cord, what should the crew do with the cord itself?
options: Leave it out and push the baby up the vagina to relieve pressure
Push the cord back into the vagina and hold it there
Clamp the cord in two places and cut between them
Wrap the cord in warm saline gauze and apply traction
questions.explanation: The cord is never pushed back. A gloved hand gently but firmly elevates the presenting part several inches to take pressure off the cord, and the crew assesses for a pulse in the cord.

questions.title: Delivery Complications
questions.stem: During labor, an arm or leg presents through the vagina. What is this an indication for?
options: Delivery on scene with fundal pressure
Manual reduction of the presenting limb
questions.explanation: A limb presentation cannot be delivered in the field, so it is an indication for immediate transport; the crew also assesses the cord for a pulse if it is prolapsed.

questions.title: Delivery Complications
questions.stem: In a breech delivery, within what time must the head deliver before suffocation can occur?
questions.explanation: Once the body has delivered, the cord is compressed and the undelivered head occludes the airway; suffocation can occur if the head is not delivered within 3 minutes.

questions.title: Delivery Complications
questions.stem: How is an airspace created for a breech baby whose head has not yet delivered?
options: Form a V with the fingers either side of the nose and push the vaginal wall away
Insert an oropharyngeal airway into the baby's mouth
Apply suprapubic pressure to lift the head off the face
Suction the oropharynx with a bulb syringe
questions.explanation: A gloved hand is placed in the vagina palm toward the baby's face, and the fingers form a V on either side of the nose to hold the vaginal wall off the face so the infant can breathe.

questions.title: Delivery Complications
questions.stem: In a breech delivery, what is the Pinard manoeuvre?
options: Abduct the hip, flex the knee and sweep the foot and leg medially to deliver it
Rotate the trunk so the back is anterior and apply downward traction
Hook an index finger over the shoulder and sweep the arm across the chest
Flex the maternal hips until the thighs touch the abdomen
questions.explanation: Pinard is used after spontaneous delivery to the umbilicus when the legs have not delivered: push laterally on the inner knee to abduct the hip, flex the knee and sweep the leg down and out, then repeat on the other side.

questions.title: Delivery Complications
questions.stem: What is the initial manoeuvre for shoulder dystocia?
options: Flex the maternal hips and legs until the thighs touch the abdomen
Rotate the anterior shoulder out of the AP diameter of the pelvis
Deliver the posterior arm by sweeping it across the fetal chest
Apply firm downward traction on the fetal head
questions.explanation: McRoberts — hyperflexing the maternal hips — rotates the symphysis and frees the impacted shoulder, and is tried first. Rotation of the anterior shoulder and delivery of the posterior arm are the additional manoeuvres if McRoberts fails.

questions.title: Delivery Complications
questions.stem: During the McRoberts manoeuvre for shoulder dystocia, what pressure should an assistant apply?
options: Downward traction on the fetal head
questions.explanation: Suprapubic pressure pushes the impacted anterior shoulder off the symphysis. Fundal pressure drives the shoulder harder into the pelvis and traction on the head risks a brachial plexus injury.

questions.title: Delivery Complications
questions.stem: Which action should be avoided once a shoulder dystocia is suspected?
options: Forcible rotation or traction on the fetal head
Flexing the maternal hips and legs
Delivering the posterior arm across the chest
questions.explanation: Forcible rotation or traction on the head overstretches the neck and causes Erb's palsy. The guideline directs a planned sequence of manoeuvres using maternal expulsive effort instead.

questions.title: Delivery Complications
questions.stem: After delivery of the infant, how long should crews wait for spontaneous delivery of the placenta?
questions.explanation: The placenta is given up to 30 minutes to deliver on its own. With minimal bleeding no aggressive attempt at removal is needed before transport, and the cord is never pulled.

questions.title: Delivery Complications
questions.stem: After the placenta delivers, how often should fundal height and firmness be checked?
options: Every 15 minutes for the first hour
Every 5 minutes for the first hour
Every 30 minutes for the first hour
Every 15 minutes for the first two hours
questions.explanation: Fundal massage is performed after delivery of the placenta until the uterus is firm, and fundal height and firmness are then rechecked every 15 minutes for the first hour, when atony is most likely.

questions.title: Delivery Complications
questions.stem: A mother with a prolapsed cord shows signs of hypoperfusion. What fluid bolus is given at the ALS level?
questions.explanation: A 250 mL bolus is given and may be repeated up to a total of 1 L provided there is no evidence of pulmonary edema; vascular access is otherwise kept at KVO or as a saline lock.

questions.title: Delivery Complications
questions.stem: After the cord is clamped in a vertex or breech delivery, what oxytocin regimen is given?
options: 20 units in 1000 mL NS/LR, 500 mL wide open then 100 mL/hr
40 units in 1 L NS/LR, 500 mL over 10 minutes
20 units in 500 mL NS/LR, run at 100 mL/hr
40 units in 1000 mL NS/LR, run wide open
questions.explanation: Oxytocin 20 units is added to 1000 mL of NS/LR, run wide open for 500 mL and then at 100 mL/hr, to facilitate placental delivery, contract the uterus and assist in tamponade. The 40-unit regimen belongs to uterine inversion.

questions.title: Delivery Complications
questions.stem: Once an inverted uterus has been replaced, what oxytocin regimen is given?
options: 40 units in 1 L NS/LR, 500 mL over 10 minutes
20 units in 1000 mL NS/LR, 500 mL wide open
40 units in 1 L NS/LR, run at 100 mL/hr
20 units in 1 L NS/LR, 500 mL over 10 minutes
questions.explanation: Uterine relaxants are stopped the moment the uterus is replaced, then oxytocin 40 units in 1 L of NS/LR is run 500 mL over 10 minutes to contract the uterus and prevent re-inversion.

questions.title: Delivery Complications
questions.stem: For uterine inversion, what nitroglycerin dose should crews discuss with the receiving physician?
questions.explanation: Nitroglycerin 50 mcg IV is used as a uterine relaxant to allow replacement of a contracted inverted uterus, and only after consultation with the receiving physician.

questions.title: Delivery Complications
questions.stem: Manual replacement of an inverted uterus falls outside whose scope of practice?
questions.explanation: The Delivery Complications guideline states manual replacement is not within the paramedic scope of practice; it is also extremely painful, so analgesia or anxiolysis should be considered when it is performed.

questions.title: Delivery Complications
questions.stem: Which breech type accounts for 50 to 70 percent of breech fetuses at term?
questions.explanation: Frank breech — both hips flexed with both knees extended so the feet lie beside the head — is the commonest. Complete breech accounts for 5 to 10 percent and incomplete for 10 to 40 percent.

questions.title: Delivery Complications
questions.stem: In delivery complications, how is a nuchal cord defined?
options: A cord that passes 360 degrees around the fetal neck
A cord that presents ahead of the fetus through the cervix
A cord that is compressed between the fetal head and the pelvis
A cord that is knotted on itself during descent
questions.explanation: A nuchal cord is one complete 360 degree loop around the neck, which is distinct from a prolapsed cord presenting ahead of the fetus.

questions.title: General OB Care and Transport Considerations
questions.stem: Beyond what cervical dilation must the crew consult the patient's RN or sending provider before accepting an obstetric transport?
questions.explanation: Greater than 5 cm dilated, or 100% effaced, means delivery may occur en route, so the appropriateness of transport must be confirmed with the sending RN or provider before the patient is accepted.

questions.title: General OB Care and Transport Considerations
questions.stem: Which examination are LFN clinicians not to perform on an obstetric patient?
questions.explanation: Digital pelvic exams are prohibited at every care level for obstetric patients. The crew inspects the perineum visually for bleeding, fluid and colour instead.

questions.title: General OB Care and Transport Considerations
questions.stem: Which findings are signs and symptoms of imminent delivery?
options: Sensation of impending defecation, urge to push, crowning
Ruptured membranes, regular contractions, back pain
Edema, headache, right upper quadrant tenderness
questions.explanation: These three findings mean delivery should be allowed to complete before transport, with newborn resuscitation initiated on scene rather than in the back of an aircraft.

questions.title: General OB Care and Transport Considerations
questions.stem: What oxygen saturation should be maintained in the obstetric patient prior to transport?
questions.explanation: General OB care sets supplemental oxygen to hold the saturation above 92%; the Delivery Complications guideline uses a 94% to 99% target during an active delivery complication.

questions.title: General OB Care and Transport Considerations
questions.stem: How should the gravid patient be positioned for transport?
options: Wedge under the right hip to maintain a left lateral lift
Wedge under the left hip to maintain a right lateral lift
questions.explanation: A wedge under the right hip tilts the patient left and takes the gravid uterus off the inferior vena cava, preserving venous return and cardiac output.

questions.title: General OB Care and Transport Considerations
questions.stem: What betamethasone dose is given to a patient at risk of preterm delivery?
questions.explanation: Betamethasone 12 mg IM is given once, per order of the sending or receiving provider, to accelerate fetal lung maturity.

questions.title: General OB Care and Transport Considerations
questions.stem: For which obstetric patients is betamethasone indicated?
options: EGA 24 0/7 to 36 6/7 weeks with risk of preterm delivery within 7 days
EGA 27 weeks or more with severe preeclampsia
EGA less than 35 weeks at the time of delivery
questions.explanation: The window is an estimated gestational age between 24 0/7 and 36 6/7 weeks with a risk of delivery inside 7 days, and it is withheld if the patient has already had a course of steroids.

questions.title: General OB Care and Transport Considerations
questions.stem: During obstetric transport, how often should the fetal heart rate be documented?
questions.explanation: Assessment and management must include maternal vital signs and oxygen saturation plus a documented fetal heart rate every 15 minutes.

questions.title: HELLP Syndrome
questions.stem: What does the acronym HELLP stand for?
options: Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets
Hypertension, Edema, Liver failure, Low Platelets
Hypoxia, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Perfusion
questions.explanation: HELLP is hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets — which explains the epigastric or right upper quadrant pain, jaundice and coagulopathic bleeding listed in the assessment column.

questions.title: HELLP Syndrome
questions.stem: How is HELLP syndrome treated?
options: Per the preeclampsia guidelines regardless of the blood pressure
Per the preeclampsia guidelines only if the SBP exceeds 160
Per the sepsis and septic shock guideline
Per the seizure guideline until delivery
questions.explanation: HELLP is a variant of severe preeclampsia, so preeclampsia treatment applies even when the patient is normotensive — which 10 to 20 percent of HELLP patients are.

questions.title: HELLP Syndrome
questions.stem: In assessing a patient for HELLP syndrome, what blood pressure indicates severe preeclampsia?
questions.explanation: Severe preeclampsia is listed as SBP above 160 or DBP above 110 with proteinuria, edema and seizures. The 180/105 and 220/120 figures belong to the ischemic stroke BP algorithm.

questions.title: HELLP Syndrome
questions.stem: At what gestational age does HELLP syndrome typically occur?
questions.explanation: HELLP typically occurs at 27 weeks gestation or later, although it occurs before 27 weeks in approximately 10 percent of cases.

questions.title: HELLP Syndrome
questions.stem: How long after delivery can signs and symptoms of HELLP syndrome first appear?
options: Up to seven days after delivery
questions.explanation: Postpartum HELLP usually presents within the first 48 hours, but signs and symptoms may appear up to seven days after delivery — so a recently delivered patient with RUQ pain still warrants suspicion.

questions.title: HELLP Syndrome
questions.stem: Which blood products should CCT crews consider for a patient with HELLP syndrome?
options: Platelets, PRBCs and plasma per order of the sending or receiving physician
Cryoprecipitate and factor concentrate on standing order
Whole blood only, after consultation with medical control
Platelets alone, once the count is known to be below 50,000
questions.explanation: Thrombocytopenia and hemolysis mean platelet, red cell and plasma transfusion may all be needed, but each is given per order of the sending or receiving physician rather than on standing order.

questions.title: Neonatal Resuscitation
questions.stem: During neonatal resuscitation, in what order is a newborn bulb suctioned?
options: Both nares first, then the oropharynx
Nares only, leaving the mouth undisturbed
Oropharynx only, leaving the nares undisturbed
questions.explanation: The mouth is suctioned before the nose so that stimulating the nares does not cause a gasp that aspirates oropharyngeal secretions.

questions.title: Neonatal Resuscitation
questions.stem: Why is caution needed when suctioning a newborn?
options: Vagus nerve stimulation causes neonatal bradycardia
It increases the risk of meconium aspiration
It causes laryngospasm in preterm infants
It strips surfactant from the upper airway
questions.explanation: Posterior pharyngeal stimulation triggers a vagal response and bradycardia in the newborn, which is why routine suctioning is avoided in a vigorous infant.

questions.title: Neonatal Resuscitation
questions.stem: On what should initial resuscitation of a newborn of 35 weeks gestation or more begin?
questions.explanation: Term and near-term newborns start on room air; those under 35 weeks start on room air up to 30% oxygen, with oxygen titrated to preductal saturation targets.

questions.title: Neonatal Resuscitation
questions.stem: On what should resuscitation of a newborn under 35 weeks gestation begin?
questions.explanation: Preterm infants begin on room air to 30% oxygen; preductal (right hand) saturations then guide titration using the target saturation table.

questions.title: Neonatal Resuscitation
questions.stem: A newborn responds poorly to ventilation and chest compressions. What IV or IO epinephrine dose is given?
questions.explanation: The preferred IV/IO dose is 0.2 mL/kg (0.02 mg/kg) of the 0.1 mg/mL concentration, within the NRP acceptable range of 0.1 – 0.3 mL/kg, followed by a 3 mL normal saline flush. The 1 mL/kg dose is the ETT route.

questions.title: Neonatal Resuscitation
questions.stem: A newborn needs epinephrine but there is no IV or IO access. What dose of the 0.1 mg/mL concentration is given via the endotracheal tube?
questions.explanation: Endotracheal absorption is poor and unreliable, so the ETT dose is five times the IV/IO dose at 1 mL/kg of the 0.1 mg/mL concentration. IV or IO remains the preferred route.

questions.title: Neonatal Resuscitation
questions.stem: During neonatal resuscitation, what flush follows epinephrine?
questions.explanation: A 3 mL normal saline flush clears the small drug volume through the umbilical or IO line into the circulation, where it would otherwise sit in the dead space.

questions.title: Neonatal Resuscitation
questions.stem: In neonatal resuscitation, after how long with no heart rate response, despite all steps being effectively completed, should redirection of care be discussed?
questions.explanation: If every step has been correctly performed and there is still no heart rate response at 20 minutes, redirection of care is discussed with the team and the family.

questions.title: Neonatal Resuscitation
questions.stem: In neonatal resuscitation, at what heart rate are chest compressions started?
questions.explanation: A heart rate below 100 triggers ventilation corrective steps; it is a rate below 60 after those steps that triggers intubation or a laryngeal mask, compressions, 100% oxygen and UVC or IO access.

questions.title: Neonatal Resuscitation
questions.stem: What compression-to-ventilation ratio is used in neonatal resuscitation?
questions.explanation: Neonatal arrest is almost always respiratory in origin, so compressions are coordinated 3:1 with ventilation rather than using the adult or child ratios.

questions.title: Neonatal Resuscitation
questions.stem: During neonatal resuscitation, what is the preductal oxygen saturation target at 5 minutes of life?
questions.explanation: The target saturation table climbs gradually: 65–70% at 2 minutes, 70–75% at 3, 75–80% at 4, 80–85% at 5 and 85–95% at 10 minutes, measured on the right hand.

questions.title: Neonatal Resuscitation
questions.stem: In the MR. SOPA ventilation corrective steps for neonatal resuscitation, what do the S and the O stand for?
options: Suction mouth and nose, then Open the mouth
Suction the airway, then place an Oral airway
questions.explanation: MR. SOPA is Mask adjustment, Reposition the head, Suction mouth and nose, Open the mouth, Pressure increase, and Alternative airway, with 5 breaths and a chest movement check after each step.

questions.title: Neonatal Resuscitation
questions.stem: During the MR. SOPA pressure step of neonatal resuscitation, what maximum ventilation pressure is recommended in a term baby?
questions.explanation: Pressure is increased incrementally by 5 to 10 cm H2O when there is no chest movement, with 40 cm H2O the maximum recommended in a term baby before moving to an alternative airway.

questions.title: Neonatal Resuscitation
questions.stem: What endotracheal tube size is used for a newborn over 2,200 g and more than 34 weeks gestation?
questions.explanation: The table runs 2.5 mm ID below 1,200 g, 3.0 mm ID for 1,201 – 2,200 g at 28 – 34 weeks, and 3.5 mm ID above 2,200 g beyond 34 weeks.

questions.title: Neonatal Resuscitation
questions.stem: What initial endotracheal tube insertion depth at the gum is used for a 30 to 32 week infant?
questions.explanation: The tip-to-gum table gives 7.0 cm at 30 – 32 weeks (1,100 – 1,400 g), rising roughly 0.5 cm per two weeks of gestation to 9.0 cm at 41 – 43 weeks.
